To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the management of certain cardiovascular conditions in the primary care sector can be achieved by the integration of general practitioners and specialists into multidimensional teams.

a collaborative, multi-disciplinary approach is required for high quality outcomes from primary care cardiovascular care, and that a collaborative, multispecialty approach is likely to lead better patient survival.

Shared care for patients with chronic health conditions can achieve the same outcomes as hospital based specialist care, if appropriately organised; andShared care for patients after hospital discharge for heart failure can achieve better outcomes than care by GPs alone, but only if the specialist is actively involved in the patient’s care.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new model of care for cardiovascular patients, in which the GP acts as a coordinator of care for the patient, with the support of a multidisciplinary team.
the organisation of services for patients with cardiovascular problems in primary care, in particular with the transfer of care for some patients from secondary care to primary care.
the organisation of care for patients with cardiovascular problems in the community, and the transfer of such services to the primary care setting.

the best care for people with cardiovascular problems is achieved when there is a collaborative, multidirectional relationship between GPs and specialists, and a multidisciplinary approach in which the patient is the focus of the care.

the transfer of patients with cardiovascular disorders from secondary to primary health care should only occur in a planned way, and that the transfer should be to a specialist-generalist multidimensional team, with a focus on the needs of the patient and the local health care system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the organisation of services for patients with cardiovascular disorders in the community should be a collaborative multidisciplinary effort.

the organisation of care for cardiovascular problems in primary care should be based on multidisciplinary teams involving both specialists and primary carers, with shared care and a focus on the management of chronic conditions.

a collaborative, interdisciplinary approach to the management of patients with chronic conditions is more likely to achieve high quality and safe outcomes for patients than a simple transfer of care to primary care.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a collaborative, multi-disciplinary approach is required for safe and cost-effective care in the primary health care setting.

there are no clear answers to the question of what works best in shifting services for people with chronic cardiovascular problems from specialist to primary care, and the answer will depend on the context and the nature of the service being provided.
a multidisciplinary team-based model of care is required for the management of patients with cardiovascular disease.
